label: explain2-track-2
one_line: We test whether a published formula for how fast a ring of gut bacteria spreads in jelly holds on data it never saw. Verdict so far: not decided yet.
what: Where things stand: the test is not finished. We have no verdict on the formula yet. We do not have enough unseen data to say if it holds or fails. Here is what we are doing. Track 2 studies a ring of living bacteria called E. coli. The bacteria start from one spot in a dish of soft jelly. The ring moves outward at a steady speed, a few millimetres each hour. A millimetre is about the thickness of a coin. A published formula says how that speed should depend on how fast the cells divide. We write down what the formula predicts before we open the measurements. Then we compare. We also fit a very simple rule as a baseline. A baseline is a plain rule that a better idea has to beat. Our aim is not a new fact about bacteria. We want a fair, repeatable check of a named rule. We also want an honest record of where it holds and where it breaks.
why: Scientists often write a rule for how a living pattern forms. Few check that rule on data they did not use to build it. This track is a small, clean test of that habit. The bacteria are only a test case. If the rule fails, we say so. If it holds only in some conditions, we say which ones. We can reuse the same method on other patterns.

steps.text: Pick the system. Gut bacteria spread from a spot in soft jelly. The jelly is loose enough for the cells to swim through.
steps.picture: A drop of ink in thin gel, except the ink is alive and can steer.

steps.text: Name what we measure. One number is how fast the outer edge of the colony moves. That edge looks like a moving ring. We give its speed in millimetres per hour. The other number is how fast the cells divide.
steps.picture: The speed of a spreading crowd, and how quickly the crowd is having babies.

steps.text: Understand the effect. Sometimes the jelly holds a little food-like chemical. The cells eat it, so the amount of chemical changes from place to place. That change is a slope. The cells can sense it and swim up it. This steering is why a ring forms at the edge. Scientists call this steering chemotaxis.
steps.picture: A crowd following a smell trail that it lays down itself.

steps.text: Set the plain-spreading baseline. Cells that only divide and wander at random would spread at a known, slower speed. This known speed is called the Fisher wave speed. It is named after the scientist who worked it out in 1937.
steps.picture: A slow walk in a random direction, used as the speed to beat.

steps.text: Write down the formula. It says the speed grows with the square root of the division rate. It also says the speed does not depend on how fast cells eat the chemical.
steps.picture: A recipe card that says which dials matter and which do not.

steps.text: Fit a simple rule on six normal measurements. It says speed squared is a fixed multiple of the division rate. It has no biology in it.
steps.picture: A rule of thumb used as a bar to clear.

steps.text: Write the predictions down and date them. We do this before we open the unseen measurements. Those are measurements we keep sealed so they can test us fairly.
steps.picture: Sealing your guess in an envelope before the race.

steps.text: Open the unseen data and compare. Mark each prediction as holding, failing, or too uncertain to say. We have not reached the end of this step yet.
steps.picture: Opening the envelope and marking it in front of everyone.

steps.text: Check the checkers. Other people recompute our sums from the public files. We also check how strict each pass-or-fail rule really is.
steps.picture: A second person re-weighing the ingredients.

wrong_if: Here is the bet, written before looking. Suppose the formula is right. Then doubling the division rate should raise the speed by only about 41 percent. That is what the square-root rule means. Some earlier project numbers hint at something else. They hint that doubling the division rate might double the speed. If the unseen data show an effect near a doubling, the formula is wrong for this system. The range of doubt must also leave out the square-root value. The range of doubt is the span of values the data cannot rule out. We have not yet seen enough data to say. One set of points so far is too weak to settle it.
could_go_wrong: Our unseen data are only unopened by us. The published paper figures may already show them. So the test is not fully blind.

Some of our pass-or-fail rules are too loose. For example, one rule counts a match if the prediction lands within 15 percent of the measurement. If the measurements themselves wobble by more than that, the rule cannot tell good from bad. A right formula could then fail, and a wrong one could pass.
One key measurement rests on only two or three dishes per point. So we cannot be very sure of it.

Every experiment we use has the same jelly firmness. Speed drops sharply when the jelly gets firmer. So firmness could be a hidden factor. A hidden factor changes the result but is not tracked in the data.
A 2024 study found that the usual equations for cells following a chemical fail when cells are very crowded. Our data may sit in that crowded zone.
That 2024 study used a narrow channel, not jelly. We do not know whether its finding carries over.
Some numbers depend on how we read the units in a file. The file does not state them.
We checked the formula's exact form only in the paper text. We did not work it out again ourselves.

questions.q: What is the verdict so far?
questions.a: There is none yet. We do not have enough unseen data to say if the square-root formula holds or fails. The simple baseline held on only 7 of 17 unseen conditions. So the test is still open.

questions.q: How do you know the ring really is faster than plain spreading?
questions.a: The paper reports that steering along a self-made slope speeds the ring up. Our own sums agree. The measured speeds are 2.49 to 7.59 times the plain-spreading speed across 25 conditions.

questions.q: How do you know your sums are right?
questions.a: Independent checkers re-ran them from the public files. The slopes, the baseline fit and the speed ratios came out the same.

We did not work out the formula again from the paper's equations. We did not open the large archive of microscope images. These are sharp-focus pictures of the spreading bacteria. We did not test other labs. We found no public data from a fully independent lab.

questions.q: Why not just use the data to fit the formula?
questions.a: A rule tuned on the data will always fit it. Only a prediction made first can fail. A test that can fail is worth something.
Only partly. It fits six normal measurements. Then it lands within 15 percent on just 7 of 17 others. The errors run from 7.8 to 94 percent.

Yes. A 2024 paper says the usual equations break when cells are packed tightly. Those equations are called the Patlak-Keller-Segel model. The paper proposes a fix. It tested a narrow channel, so how well it fits jelly is unknown.

questions.q: What is the library of laws, and does it already cover this?
questions.a: It is our list of rules, each written as a short maths statement. A computer program called Lean checks each statement line by line. Think of a spell-checker, but for algebra. The library has no checked rule for steered rings. The nearest one is for plain spreading, the Fisher wave speed. It is only a candidate, which means not yet fully accepted. It also gives only a lower bound. That means the real speed should be at least that fast. It does not give the exact speed. The library comes in numbered releases. We used release 1.8.1.

questions.q: Is the new square-root law proven?
questions.a: No. A computer checked the maths of the statement. That shows the algebra has no slips. It does not show that real bacteria follow the law.

questions.q: What does the 'straight doubling' hint mean?
questions.a: Some earlier project numbers suggest that doubling the division rate may double the speed. The square-root formula says it should rise by only about 41 percent. We do not yet know which is right.

glossary.plain: A common bacterium that lives in the gut of people and animals.
A jelly made from seaweed. It is so loose that bacteria can swim through it.
The outer edge of the spreading colony. It looks like a moving ring.
A chemical, like a faint smell of food, that cells swim towards.
A slope in the amount of that chemical, rising from one place to the next. Cells swim up it.
Swimming up or down a chemical slope.
How fast an amount changes from one place to the next.
How quickly the cells divide.
The number that gives your number when multiplied by itself. The square root of 4 is 2.
A short written rule that links numbers to each other.
A simple rule used as the bar that a better idea must beat.
A result we write down before looking at the data.
Measurements we keep sealed and unopened. They let us test a prediction fairly.
Spread by dividing and wandering at random, with no steering.
The known speed of a front driven only by growth and random wandering. Named after the scientist Fisher, 1937.
The usual set of equations for how cells follow a chemical. Named after three sets of scientists.
A rule in our library that is not yet fully accepted.
A floor. The true speed should be at least this fast, maybe more.
The span of values the data cannot rule out.
Something that changes the result but is not tracked in the data.
A set of equations that stands in for a real system.
How tightly packed the cells are.
A crowd of bacteria grown from one starting spot.
Our list of rules whose maths a computer has checked line by line.
One numbered release of that library. We used release 1.8.1.
A computer program that checks mathematical proofs line by line, like a spell-checker for algebra.
A line we draw in advance. For example, a prediction passes if it lands within 15 percent of the measurement.
A kind of microscope that takes sharp-focus pictures. The large image archive in this track came from one.
A saved set of measurements.
A thousandth of a metre, about the thickness of a coin.
Slow random spreading, like a smell drifting through a room.

check_yourself.what: Check the first source paper exists and has the title shown
check_yourself.expect: The title Chemotaxis as a navigation strategy to boost range expansion.

check_yourself.what: Find the square-root sentence in the second paper
check_yourself.command: curl https://www.ebi.ac.uk/europepmc/webservices/rest/PMC8640786/fullTextXML and search for 'square root dependence on the growth rate'
check_yourself.expect: A sentence in the results section that says speed depends on the square root of the growth rate.

check_yourself.what: Redo the baseline fit and the speed ratios
check_yourself.expect: A fitted constant of 16.904, and 7 of 17 other conditions within 15 percent.

check_yourself.what: Compare the plain-spreading speed with the measured one
check_yourself.expect: Ratios from 2.49 to 7.59 times the plain-spreading speed.

check_yourself.what: Check the Phan 2024 claim about crowded cells
check_yourself.expect: An abstract saying the older model breaks down at high cell densities.

check_yourself.what: Confirm our law library has no steered-front law

left_out: Phan 2024 as the 'strongest' rival: only partly supported, so it is described as a rival, not the best one.
The claim that every frozen number is correct and the problem is only the rules: only partly supported, so it is not stated as a fact.

That one prediction (the e-fold length) is 'sound' with a 1 percent correction and 3 to 5 percent spread: not recomputed by the checkers, so left out. The reader did not know the term, so it is no longer mentioned at all.
Power figures for the speed-independence test and the claim that a plateau test cannot fail: the agent's own analysis, only partly checked.
The 150 MB size cap and which predictions need the big image archive: project rules, not checkable, so not given as fact.
The advice to keep, add or drop particular datasets: a recommendation, not a checkable claim.
Median ratio of 4.73 and the 4.4 to 5.4 wild-type ratios: not in the verified list, so only the 2.49 to 7.59 range is used.
The 6-of-14-within-15-percent figure: not verified, so the checked 7-of-17 figure is used instead.
We do not know how much the measurements wobble compared with the 15 percent line, so the text gives no number for it.
